topics.name: Place value
facts: Each digit in a number has a value determined by its position (column).
Place value columns from right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands, millions.
After the decimal point, columns are: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
The digit 0 is a place holder — it keeps other digits in the correct column.
Moving a digit one place to the left multiplies its value by 10.
Moving a digit one place to the right divides its value by 10.
To compare numbers, compare digits from the highest place value first.
1 million = 1,000,000 (six zeros).

retrieval_questions.q: What is the value of the digit 7 in the number 4,752?
What is the value of the digit 3 in 0.235?
Write the number three thousand four hundred and six in digits.
What does the digit 0 do in the number 305?
retrieval_questions.a: Acts as a place holder (in the tens column)

retrieval_questions.q: What is 6,492 rounded to the nearest thousand? (place value reading)

topics.name: Rounding
facts: To round, look at the digit immediately after the place you're rounding to.
If that digit is 5 or more, round up; if less than 5, round down.
Rounding to the nearest 10: look at the ones digit.
Rounding to the nearest 100: look at the tens digit.
Rounding to the nearest 1000: look at the hundreds digit.
To round to 1 decimal place, look at the hundredths digit.
Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit.
When rounding, fill the lower place values with zeros where needed (for whole numbers).

topics.name: Linear sequences
facts: A linear sequence increases or decreases by the same amount each time (the common difference).
The common difference is found by subtracting any term from the next term.
The nth term rule has the form: an + b, where a is the common difference.
To find b, subtract the common difference from the first term.
To find a term in a sequence, substitute the position number into the nth term rule.
An arithmetic sequence is the same as a linear sequence.
If the sequence is decreasing, the common difference (a) is negative.

topics.name: Calculating with fractions
facts: To add or subtract fractions, they must have a common denominator.
To multiply fractions, multiply numerators together and denominators together.
To divide fractions, multiply by the reciprocal (flip the second fraction and multiply).
Always simplify (cancel) fractions to their lowest terms.
Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing.
An improper fraction has a numerator larger than its denominator.
A mixed number has a whole number part and a fraction part.

topics.name: Fraction of an amount
facts: To find a unit fraction of an amount, divide by the denominator.
To find a non-unit fraction (e.g. 3/5) of an amount, divide by the denominator then multiply by the numerator.
'Of' in maths means multiply.
1/2 of an amount means divide by 2.
1/4 of an amount means divide by 4.
To find 3/4 of 20: divide 20 by 4 (=5), then multiply by 3 (=15).

topics.name: Percentage of an amount
facts: 'Per cent' means 'out of 100'.
10% of an amount = divide by 10.
1% of an amount = divide by 100.
To find 5%, find 10% and halve it.
To find any percentage, find 10% and 1% and build up.
Multiplier method: x% = ÷100 then ×x (e.g. 30% = ×0.3).

topics.name: Reading number lines
facts: Count the divisions between two labelled values on a number line.
Work out the size of each interval = (difference between labels) ÷ (number of divisions).
Number lines can show decimals, fractions, and negative numbers.
Numbers to the left are smaller; numbers to the right are larger.
The midpoint between two numbers is their average ((a + b) ÷ 2).
On a number line, equal spacing means equal value differences.

topics.name: Pictograms
facts: A pictogram uses pictures or symbols to represent data.
A pictogram always needs a key showing what one symbol represents.
Half a symbol represents half the value of the key.
Count symbols and multiply by the key value to find totals.
Pictograms are best for comparing categories of data.
The key should be checked carefully before reading values.

retrieval_questions.q: What do you call the symbol on a pictogram that tells you how much each picture represents?

topics.name: Bar charts
facts: A bar chart uses bars of equal width to represent data values by their height.
Each bar represents a category; gaps between bars are equal.
The vertical axis shows frequency (or value); the horizontal axis shows categories.
Always label axes clearly and include a title.
Read the value of a bar by looking across from the top to the vertical axis.
A dual bar chart compares two sets of data side-by-side using two bars per category.
Bar charts are used for discrete or categorical data.

retrieval_questions.q: What two things should every bar chart have on its axes?
Should there be gaps between bars on a bar chart?
What does the height of a bar represent?
What is a bar chart that compares two data sets called?

Why must all bars on a bar chart be the same width?
retrieval_questions.a: So heights can be fairly compared

topics.name: Solving one and two step equations
facts: An equation has an equals sign and can be solved to find an unknown.
Whatever you do to one side, do the same to the other to keep balance.
Use inverse operations to undo what is happening to the variable.
Inverse of + is -; inverse of × is ÷ (and vice versa).
For two-step equations, undo addition/subtraction first, then multiplication/division.
Always check your answer by substituting back into the original equation.
Aim to isolate the variable on one side.

topics.name: Calculating with directed number
facts: Directed numbers are positive and negative numbers.
Adding a negative is the same as subtracting (+ - = -).
Subtracting a negative is the same as adding (- - = +).
Two same signs multiplied/divided give a positive result.
Two different signs multiplied/divided give a negative result.
Negative × negative = positive.
Negative × positive = negative.
On a number line, moving left = subtracting; moving right = adding.

topics.name: Simplifying algebraic expressions
facts: Like terms have the same variable raised to the same power.
Only like terms can be added or subtracted (collected together).
Coefficients are the numbers in front of variables (e.g. 5 in 5x).
x × x = x² (x squared).
When multiplying terms, multiply the numbers and combine the letters.
ab is the same as a × b.
x means 1x (the coefficient 1 is not written).
3x + 2x = 5x (collect like terms by adding coefficients).

retrieval_questions.q: What is the coefficient of x in 7x?

retrieval_questions.a: Terms with the same variables to the same powers

topics.name: Converting between fractions, decimals and percentages
facts: To convert a fraction to a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator.
To convert a decimal to a percentage, multiply by 100.
To convert a percentage to a decimal, divide by 100.
To convert a percentage to a fraction, write it over 100 and simplify.

retrieval_questions.q: Convert 40% to a fraction in its simplest form.
Convert 0.8 to a fraction in simplest form.

topics.name: Estimation
facts: To estimate, round each number to 1 significant figure.
Use ≈ (approximately equal to) when estimating.
Estimating is used to check whether an answer is sensible.
Estimate before calculating to spot mistakes.
Round numbers to convenient values that are easy to calculate with.
An estimate is not exact but should be close to the actual answer.

retrieval_questions.q: Why do we estimate before calculating?
retrieval_questions.a: To check the answer is sensible

topics.name: Order of operations
facts: BIDMAS: Brackets, Indices, Division/Multiplication, Addition/Subtraction.
Division and multiplication have equal priority — work left to right.
Addition and subtraction have equal priority — work left to right.
Always do operations inside brackets first.
Indices (powers) come after brackets.
BIDMAS is sometimes called BODMAS (O for Of/Order).
Use brackets to make order of operations clear.

retrieval_questions.q: Which has higher priority: indices or multiplication?

topics.name: Area and perimeter of 2D shapes
facts: Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a 2D shape (units like cm).
Area is the amount of space a 2D shape covers (square units like cm²).
Area of a rectangle = length × width.
Area of a square = side × side (or side²).
Area of a triangle = (base × height) ÷ 2.
Area of a parallelogram = base × perpendicular height.
Area of a trapezium = ½ × (a + b) × h, where a and b are the parallel sides.
Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 × (length + width).
For compound shapes, split into simpler shapes and add areas.
Always include correct units: cm for perimeter, cm² for area.
